title: The trustworthy
hookLine: Mecca calls him al-Amin and al-Sadiq, the trustworthy and the truthful

lines: SMALL THINGS, DONE THE SAME WAY.
cards: Some reputations are built by speeches. This one, as the sirah tells it, was built the slow way, in the ordinary dealings of a trading town: what a person says, what a person keeps, what a person gives back.

By the time the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is a grown man in Mecca, the sirah says, people have stopped using only his name. They call him by what he is to them: a title given not by a king, but by neighbors and traders.

teach.b: Ibn Ishaq says Quraysh called him al-Amin, the trustworthy. Tradition remembers him too as al-Sadiq, the truthful.
Two words, one picture: a man whose word matched what happened, and whose hands could be trusted with what wasn't his.
Muslims often point to two hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari where the praise comes from people who had turned against his message. The first comes from the day he began to call his own clans in public.
He climbs the hill of Safa and calls them by name.

When they gather, he asks: if I told you there were horsemen in the valley behind this hill, about to attack you, would you believe me? And they answer: yes, we have never known you to say anything but the truth.
Then he tells them his message, and his own uncle Abu Lahab scolds him in front of everyone. But they had already said it.
The second comes from Abu Sufyan, at the time still one of his fiercest opponents, standing before the Byzantine emperor Heraclius, who questions him about this new prophet.
Did you ever accuse him of lying, before he made his claim? And Abu Sufyan says no. In the same report he admits he'd have lied about him if he hadn't feared his companions calling him a liar.
Heraclius reasons aloud: a man who never lied about people would hardly lie about God. Both scenes come from after the revelation began, but both look back.
Even his opponents say that before the message, they had known him for his word. The trust was there first.

how: Muslims refer to the Prophet ﷺ as al-Sadiq al-Amin, the truthful and trustworthy, and honesty in speech and trade is taught as part of following his example.

o: one whose word and hands can be fully trusted
a judge chosen to settle disputes in Mecca
a chief elected by the clans of Quraysh

p: where he asked: would you believe me?
admitted he'd never been called a liar

s: the title al-Amin was given only after he became a prophet
Ibn Ishaq says Quraysh called him that before the revelation.
at Safa, his clans said they'd only known him to tell the truth
Abu Sufyan told Heraclius the Prophet had lied before
asked if he'd ever lied, his opponent said no.

games.q: he stands on the hill of Safa and asks his clans: if I said horsemen were behind this hill, would you believe me? what do they answer?
o: we'd want to see them first.
yes, we've only known you to tell the truth.
no, you're too young to judge.
games.why: al-Bukhari reports they said yes; they'd only known him to tell the truth. his uncle Abu Lahab scolded him anyway.

practice: Bring to mind a moment coming up where the easy thing is a small untruth, an excuse for being late, a compliment you don't mean, a number rounded the convenient way, and picture yourself saying the true thing instead, kindly and plainly.
Rehearse the sentence once in your head until it feels like yours. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make your word match your deed.

wordCard.voice: The trustworthy. Al-Amin, what Mecca called him, the sirah says, before any revelation came, and al-Sadiq, the truthful. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: al-Amin, the trustworthy, the one who can be given a trust.

carryVoice: Your line: known for truth. Tomorrow, Khadijah's caravan heads north. See you there.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Quraysh called him al-Amin)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4770 (Safa: would you believe me? we have only known you to tell the truth)
Sahih al-Bukhari 7 (Abu Sufyan before Heraclius: did you accuse him of lying?)
